the use of non standard floating point formats in the context of HLS allows for a more efficient implementation of the summation reduction pattern, while maintaining the ease of use and readability of the C language.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: can HLS be used as a tool to express non standard arithmetic?
the following questions: (1) How to express application specific arithmetic in HLS, (2) What are the benefits of such a compiler, and (3) What are the limitations?
a new approach for the synthesis of floating point summation reductions, which is based on non-standard arithmetic.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this work shows that HLS can be used for application specific computations, but only if one is willing to accept the limitations of the C/C++ language, and to accept the limitations that HLS tools impose on the implementation.
this work shows that the HLS approach can be extended to non standard computations.
HLS is not the right tool for the job when one wants to exploit FPGA non standard capabilities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have designed a compiler that can transform floating point summations into a form that is more suitable for FPGAs.
we have designed a source to source compiler that takes a C program as input and outputs a C++ program that is more amenable to HLS and more efficient.
HLS is a great tool, but it is not the only tool for programming FPGAS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HLS paradigm is not the only way to program FPGAs.
the IEEE floating point standard can be circumvented in a controlled manner, and that this is beneficial for HLS.
the IEEE 754 semantics of floating point operations are too restrictive to be efficiently implemented on FPGAs.
